categories.label: Labor Union Dynamics and Workforce Resistance
categories.memo: Covers how union agreements and workforce fears shape adoption of prefabrication and robotics, and how contractual/organizational responses can mitigate resistance.

codes.label: Union Resistance to Offsite/Prefabricated Work
codes.description: Labor unions, especially in electrical trades, resist prefabrication and outsourcing fabrication due to fears of reduced work hours for union labor, constraining contractor adoption decisions.

sub_codes.label: Fear of Reduced Work Hours
sub_codes.description: Union locals oppose prefabrication because it may shift labor from installation-heavy union work to offsite manufacturing, reducing billable hours for members.

sub_codes.label: Mitigation Through Experience and Catalog Framing
sub_codes.description: Contractors with existing prefabrication facilities report less union resistance; manufacturers reframe prefabricated items as 'catalog products' to comply with union constraints.

codes.label: Need for Contractual/Policy Strategies to Resolve Union-Contractor Tension
codes.description: Recommendations for formal contractual and labor policy mechanisms, such as prefabrication outsourcing agreements and labor portability between union locals, to align incentives.

codes.label: Human-Robot Collaboration in Labor Allocation
codes.description: Since robots cannot fully replace workers, contracts and staffing plans must accommodate ongoing human-robot collaboration modes on site.

categories.label: Subcontractor Financial and Risk Repositioning
categories.memo: Focuses on how MMC/off-site prefabrication alters subcontractors' scope of work, margin capture, competitive exposure, and risk allocation relative to head contractors and manufacturers.

codes.label: Loss of Value Capture and Margin Pass-Through
codes.description: Savings generated by off-site prefabrication (e.g., pods) tend to be passed up the contracting chain to head contractors rather than retained by subcontractors, due to traditional (non-relational) subcontract structures.

codes.label: Erosion of Risk Allowance in Pricing
codes.description: Off-site prefabrication removes traditional income sources (materials/labour margin) for subcontractors without corresponding adjustment of contract pricing to include a risk allowance for the new arrangement.

codes.label: Increased Competitive Exposure
codes.description: Prefabrication lowers barriers to entry, allowing smaller or non-traditional firms to bid on jobs, intensifying price competition and undermining incumbent subcontractors' position.

codes.label: Financial Risk to Lenders and Project Financing
codes.description: Modular construction's upfront automation, design, and transport costs create financing risk, including lender exposure to potential module manufacturer bankruptcy.

categories.label: Coordination, Collaboration, and Supply Chain Roles
categories.memo: Addresses the organizational relationships and coordination mechanisms needed among designers, manufacturers, subcontractors, and contractors to manage the split between offsite and onsite work.

codes.label: Supply Chain Coordination as Core Management Function
codes.description: Managing the complexity of split offsite/onsite work scope requires integral supply chain management involving vendors, distributors, manufacturers, and fabricators.

codes.label: Early Involvement and Communication Among Stakeholders
codes.description: Early and close coordination among designers, manufacturers, and contractors (or subcontractors) is a recurring success factor to avoid rework, delays, and constructability problems; breakdowns cause project friction.

codes.label: Project Manager as Onsite/Offsite Coordinator
codes.description: The project manager plays a central coordinating role bridging on-site and off-site activities, managing schedule, transport constraints, and stakeholder objectives.

codes.label: Fragmented Coordination Challenges
codes.description: The fragmented nature of modular/robotic construction creates difficulty coordinating continuous transitions between work processes, risking cost overruns and technical difficulties.

codes.label: Joint Product Development and Long-Term Partnerships
codes.description: Joint development between subcontractors and manufacturers is identified as key to successful transition to off-site technology, but such relationships remain project-based rather than long-term strategic partnerships, unlike other industries.

categories.label: Manufacturer and Vendor Role Evolution
categories.memo: Covers how manufacturers and vendors are expanding beyond traditional supply roles into active industrialization partners, and the quasi-contractual arrangements this generates.

codes.label: Manufacturer as Active Industrialization Partner
codes.description: Manufacturers increasingly provide training, customization, and catalog-based prefabricated assemblies, shifting from simple parts suppliers to active partners in the construction process.

codes.label: Expansion of Vendor Role into Material Logistics Management
codes.description: Vendors extend beyond delivery to include warehousing, logistics, and inventory control services, shifting risk and responsibility allocation on prefabrication-heavy projects.

codes.label: Nonbinding Vendor Partnership Agreements
codes.description: Vendor partnerships are formalized through nonbinding agreements covering communication, materials, delivery/returns, payment, technology, and training responsibilities, functioning as quasi-contractual arrangements supporting prefabrication.

codes.label: Manufacturer as Subcontractor in Detailed Design
codes.description: In some markets, manufacturers are institutionally limited to a subcontractor role for detailed component design, separate from the architect-led design process, constraining their integration into project delivery.

codes.label: Frequent Interfacing with Robot Manufacturers Complicating Subcontracting
codes.description: The need for frequent interfacing with construction robot manufacturers increases management complexity and complicates subcontracting arrangements.

categories.label: Workforce Skills, Competence, and Capacity Building
categories.memo: Addresses skill shortages, expertise gaps, and organizational capacity-building pathways required for firms and workers to adapt to MMC and prefabrication.

codes.label: Shortage of Skilled Labor and Expertise
codes.description: A shortage of experienced professionals in modular/prefabricated systems leads to improper procedures and substandard quality; lack of designer/manufacturer/contractor expertise generates conflicts and delays.

codes.label: Phased Capacity-Building Roadmap for Contractors
codes.description: A recommended multi-phase roadmap—from outsourcing to fabricators, to building a small facility, to full-scale operation—reflects evolving organizational and contractual relationships as contractors build prefabrication capacity.

codes.label: BIM and Digital Coordination Capability as Enabler
codes.description: BIM capability correlates with greater vendor early involvement and more manufacturer-supplied assemblies, but interoperability limitations between design and manufacturing software constrain organizational integration.

categories.label: Project Delivery System and Organizational Fit
categories.memo: Considers how project delivery method choice interacts with organizational roles and readiness for MMC/prefabrication/robotics, and gaps in current contracting systems.

codes.label: Delivery System Influence on Prefabrication Success
codes.description: Design-build is perceived as more prefabrication-friendly than other delivery systems, though many practitioners see no significant difference; IPD assists but is not a prerequisite for successful prefabrication implementation.

codes.label: Absence of Contracting Systems Adapted to Robotics
codes.description: No current construction management or contracting system is well adapted to accommodate robotic construction, indicating a structural/organizational gap that contracts must address.

codes.label: Government and Policy Incentives Driving Organizational Adoption
codes.description: Government incentive mechanisms, mandates, and contractual provisions are seen as necessary to drive contractor and industry adoption of robotics and prefabrication, especially where mature technical systems are lacking.

codes.label: Design Freeze Requirements Conflicting with Traditional Practice
codes.description: MMC/off-site prefabrication requires early design finalization, conflicting with industry norms of incomplete design and ongoing changes, creating organizational and contractual friction for design teams and subcontractors.

categories.label: Public and Industry Perception Barriers
categories.memo: Captures organizational and cultural barriers stemming from perceptions of MMC among industry participants and the public.

codes.label: Negative Stereotypes Hindering Adoption
codes.description: Perceptions of modular/prefabricated construction as cheap or limited in design options hinder broader acceptance among industry professionals and the public, affecting organizational willingness to adopt MMC.
